name: Prize crossword No 23,053
preamble: Solve the clues and fit the solutions in the diagram jigsaw-wise, wherever they will go. Because the grid is perfectly symmetrical, there are two alternatives ways of doing this. In the correct version, A and C go across, D down and Bs both ways, the first across.

clue.text: Spooner's slow cooker's stopper, bossy bird

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of two words trade places

blocks.note: a wok is an Asian cooking pan; swapping its opening sound with the next word's
caulk is a sealant that stops up gaps, and its opening sound trades with the pan's

explanation.surface: A crock-pot's lid somehow turns into a domineering bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'wok of the caulk' and swap the first sounds: 'cock of the walk'. 'Slow' is surface colour, since a wok is a fast cooker.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a domineering person who rules the roost, and a cock is literally a male bird strutting its yard.

clue.text: In one-day cricket, failed when breathalysed

blocks.note: first meaning: a limited-overs match, where each side bats for a fixed number of overs
second meaning: having more alcohol in the blood than the law allows a driver

explanation.walkthrough: One-day cricket is limited-overs cricket, each side getting a set number of overs (sets of six balls); the same two words describe a drink-driver.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorist who fails a breath test has blood alcohol beyond the legal maximum, while the cricket sense names a cap on overs bowled.

clue.text: Concept of Destiny that's made a mark

indicators.note: to make something is to construct it, so these letters are built into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An idea about fate that has left its stamp on the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made a mark' reads as a single idiom about having influence, but 'made' is the signal working on the two words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu and Buddhist thought, the sum of one's deeds determines future fortune, a notion of fate or destiny.

clue.text: Note given to Ralph by Barbara, both on stage

blocks.note: F is a musical note
Ralph Lynn was an English comic actor of the Aldwych farces

explanation.surface: A message passed from one actor to another backstage.
explanation.walkthrough: Both names are actors' first names: put a note before Ralph's surname to get Barbara's.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbara Flynn is an English stage and television actress, so her first name points to her surname here.

clue.text: Yank queen in love: for silence one must pay

indicators.note: a thing placed in another sits inside it, surrounded on both sides

blocks.note: a Yank is an American, from the US
HM stands for Her Majesty
honey is a term of endearment

explanation.surface: A monarch in an affair with an American must pay to keep it quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank' looks like a verb meaning pull, but it is the American; the two short pieces go together inside the endearment.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a bribe paid to keep someone quiet, usually about a scandal, exactly what one pays to buy silence.

clue.text: Glutton whose booze holds gun whence Rev must fly

indicators.note: what flies away leaves, so these letters are taken out
to hold something is to keep it inside, so one word goes around another

blocks.note: wine is an alcoholic drink
a revolver is a handgun
Rev is the abbreviation for Reverend, taken off the front of the gun

explanation.surface: A greedy clergyman's drink habit somehow involves a firearm, and he must flee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glutton' looks like a description of a person, but it is an old name for an animal; the gun loses its first three letters before going inside the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The wolverine's alternative name is glutton, a large carnivorous weasel of northern forests with a reputation for a voracious appetite.

clue.text: Had inclination for a fast, d'ye hark?

indicators.note: to hark is to listen, so the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting before Easter

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you felt like going without food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inclination' suggests a wish or desire, but the definition is literal: tilted.
explanation.definitionFit: To have an inclination is to be tilted at an angle, so the past tense of tilting or sloping fits.

clue.text: A tease for weight: could be the mind's the master's

definitions.text: could be the mind's the master's
definitions.note: a definition by example: the show Mastermind, read with its halves swapped

blocks.note: in older English a quiz is a hoax or a person who mocks and teases
pro means in favour of
a gramme is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A cryptic musing about a tease, a weight and whose mind belongs to the master.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The mind's the master's' is Mastermind taken apart: the long-running BBC television quiz show with its famous black chair.
explanation.definitionFit: Mastermind is a celebrated British television general-knowledge contest, one example of a broadcast question-and-answer show.

clue.text: See 13
So is the lark - you hark - at heaven's gates

definitions.text: So is the lark - you hark - at heaven's gates

blocks.clueFragment: So is the lark - you hark - at heaven's gates
blocks.note: surface reading: an echo of Shakespeare's song 'Hark, hark! the lark at heaven's gate sings', picturing the bird high in the sky
setter's reading: the lark rises at dawn, so an early riser is called a lark; the bird is also high aloft

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation comes from a song in Shakespeare's Cymbeline. The lark is both aloft at heaven's gate and the proverbial dawn riser, so both words of the answer fit it.
explanation.definitionFit: Larks sing at first light and soar high, so the bird is both out of bed at dawn and aloft in the sky.

clue.text: Disposed of trouble, one who fought in Spain

blocks.note: to dispose of goods is to sell them
ado is fuss or bother

explanation.surface: Someone who got rid of a problem, a veteran of the Spanish wars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disposed of' suggests killing or discarding, but here it means sold.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish word for a soldier, also used in English, so a fighting man in a Spanish army.

clue.text: Scott's wife's last shrub is heard (Scots disagree)

indicators.note: being heard means judged by sound; the aside admits that Scots, who sound every R, would not pronounce it this way

blocks.note: Z is the last letter of the alphabet
the elder is a shrub; in southern English the final R is silent

explanation.surface: A remark about the last bush planted by Scott's wife, with Scottish readers objecting.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald's wife was Zelda. Elder and the ending -elda only rhyme if the R is dropped, which Scots speakers do not do.
explanation.definitionFit: Zelda Sayre married the novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald, author of The Great Gatsby, and was a writer herself.

clue.text: Anaesthetist, nurse having organised a tester, is for leader authorised

indicators.note: to organise something is to arrange it, so these letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: an anaesthetist is one who numbs, so a numb-er
to nurse is to tend
having something is owning it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hospital team member rearranges an examiner and turns out to be approved for leadership.
explanation.walkthrough: An anaesthetist is read as one who numbs. Watch the word breaks: the pieces join and re-split at different points from the clue's. The address is the British Prime Minister's official London home.
explanation.definitionFit: The London house is the official residence assigned to the British Prime Minister, the country's leader.

clue.text: King holding road - record the song again

indicators.note: to hold something is to have it within one's grasp, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: Rex is Latin for king
the M1 is a British motorway, written MI in the grid

explanation.surface: A monarch blocking a street while re-recording a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds; crosswords turn its digit into the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A new version of a track made by reworking and rebalancing its recorded parts, so producing the tune afresh.

clue.text: Unknowns keep queen round duke: hence home and dry

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so a pair surrounds the other pieces

blocks.note: x and y are the usual unknowns in algebra
ER is the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth
O is round in shape
Prince Philip was the Duke of Edinburgh

explanation.surface: Mysterious figures guard a royal couple, who are then safe and finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home and dry' is a British idiom for safely finished, but here it is read literally: living where it is dry.
explanation.definitionFit: The botanical term means a liking for, or adaptation to, arid habitats, as in cacti whose natural home is desert.

clue.text: See the last first? Not I in jumble sale

indicators.note: a jumble is a muddled heap, so these letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: v stands for vide, Latin for see, in references
the end is the last part
I is the Roman numeral one, the first number
taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzled shopper at a jumble sale wondering about last and first, and denying something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See the last first' reads as an instruction to reorder, but it is three separate pieces. A jumble sale is a British charity sale of second-hand goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A rare, formal word for the act of selling, related to vend, so it means a sale.

clue.text: Of journeys made by Ivor with a tail

indicators.note: something made is constructed, so the letters are assembled afresh

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Trips undertaken by a man named Ivor, who has a tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made by' looks like a credit for Ivor, but it signals that his name and the next two words are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin viator, a traveller, the adjective means relating to travel or to people on the road.

clue.text: Turned in, rolled close - with unit loved to play

indicators.note: to play is to move freely and loosely, so these letters run about into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A team that loved to play curled up together, heading inwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is two near-synonyms run together, both botanical descriptions of a curled leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany an involute leaf has edges curled inward, so the word means curled or wound inwards on itself.

clue.text: Prepares, if year were good, for yesterday

indicators.note: imagining one letter turned into another means one is swapped out for the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Y is the abbreviation for year
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone getting ready, wishing last year had gone better, longing for the past.
explanation.walkthrough: Change a Y of 'yesterday' to G and rearrange. There is no separate shuffle signal: 'for' is the only joining word, a liberty of this setter.
explanation.definitionFit: To prepare is to make oneself fit and ready for something, a plain verb synonym in the third person.

clue.text: He strangely lives, this royal personage

indicators.note: something strange is out of its usual state, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man strangely survives, and he is a royal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He strangely lives' nods to the joke that Elvis is still alive after his death in 1977; he was called the King of rock and roll.
explanation.definitionFit: Elvis Presley was nicknamed the King, so the singer is called a royal personage, and he is a man.

clue.text: Two girls: we hear them singing side by side

indicators.note: what we hear is judged by sound, not spelling

blocks.note: two girls' names, Ann and Tiffany, said one after the other

explanation.surface: Two girls are heard performing a duet next to each other.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface seems to describe the girls singing, but they are two names, Ann and Tiffany, run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Music in which two choirs or groups sing alternate verses in response to each other, typically placed on facing sides.

clue.text: No company for Graces or for Fates

definitions.text: No company for Graces or for Fates

blocks.clueFragment: No company for Graces or for Fates
blocks.note: surface reading: the Graces and the Fates are lonely figures without companions
setter's reading: two's company, but the next number is a crowd, and it is how many Graces and how many Fates there were

explanation.walkthrough: The saying is 'two's company, three's a crowd'. In Greek myth there were three Graces and three Fates.
explanation.definitionFit: The number following two, which the proverb calls a crowd, is the count of each mythical sisterhood.

clue.text: Persist with bark for shrub producing tea

blocks.note: a yap is a dog's sharp bark
to persist is to carry on, keep on

explanation.surface: A dog keeps barking at a tea bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bark' suggests the outer layer of a plant, fitting the shrub surface, but it is a dog's noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Yapon, or yaupon, is an American holly whose leaves were brewed by Native Americans into a caffeinated drink.

clue.text: By this boat's emptied and a stack supplied

blocks.note: first meaning: a scoop for removing water from a boat, more often spelt bailer
second meaning: a farm machine that packs hay or straw into bundles for stacking

explanation.surface: A tool that drains a boat and also provides a pile of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The boat sense is usually spelt with an I, but this spelling is also accepted for the scoop.
explanation.definitionFit: One word names both a scoop for removing water from a dinghy and a machine that bundles hay for a haystack.

clue.text: Toby postprandially may be heard

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of Sir Toby, the drunken uncle in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night
second meaning: the noisy release of wind after a meal

explanation.surface: A man named Toby can be heard after dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Postprandially means after a meal. Sir Toby's surname suits his love of food and drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Toby's surname in Twelfth Night is also the word for burping, the noise one may hear after eating.

clue.text: Just swallow one: a dry one is advised

definitions.note: the whole second half describes the drink: a dry martini is the classic order

blocks.note: the house and sand birds of this name belong to the swallow family
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Advice at the bar: drink only one, and make it a dry one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallow' looks like a verb about drinking, but it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The cocktail of gin and vermouth is classically ordered dry, meaning little vermouth, so the dry drink is it.

clue.text: The painter's, not the stacker's nor the taster's

blocks.clueFragment: The painter's, not the stacker's nor the taster's
blocks.note: surface reading: three people's possessions, of which only the artist's is wanted

blocks.clueFragment: not the stacker's nor the taster's
blocks.note: setter's reading: three words sound alike; the stacker's is a pallet, the taster's a palate, and only the artist's board is meant

explanation.walkthrough: Pallet (a stacking platform) and palate (the roof of the mouth) sound the same as the answer; the clue rules them out by owner.
explanation.definitionFit: The thin board on which an artist mixes colours belongs to the painter, distinct from its sound-alike words.

clue.text: In one united gardener with park

blocks.note: Gertrude Jekyll was a famous English garden designer
with means together with, and
Hyde Park is a large royal park in central London

explanation.surface: A gardener and a park joined as one.
explanation.walkthrough: In Stevenson's story the respectable doctor and the brutal Mr Hyde are two personalities in a single body.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a person with two opposing natures, from Stevenson's tale of doctor and monster sharing one body.
